I reviewed `artifacts/editorial/release-candidates/technology/windows-11-july-update-pause-restore-controls.mdx` in full, plus its research artifact (`artifacts/editorial/research/2026-07-17-windows-11-july-update.json`) and the image on disk. One honesty note up front: my available tools in this session (Read/Grep/Glob only, no shell) cannot recompute a SHA-256, so I could not independently re-hash the file; this review applies to the single file at that exact path as read, and the verdict lines carry the hash you supplied.

## Factual support and source use
- Every load-bearing claim is explicitly attributed to Microsoft ("Microsoft says/lists/notes") and mapped to one of four primary Microsoft URLs, which match the research artifact's `sourceUrls` exactly. No claims are sourced to rumor or third-party speculation.
- **Independently verifiable facts check out**: build 26200 = 25H2 and 26100 = 24H2 is correct; the 35-day pause ceiling matches Windows Update's long-standing 5-week maximum; and the Windows 11 24H2 Home/Pro end-of-servicing date of **October 13, 2026** is correct (24-month servicing from the October 2024 GA, second Tuesday of October 2026). Point-in-time restore's described behavior (VSS-based, ~24-hour capture, ~72-hour retention, includes user files, BitLocker recovery key path) matches Microsoft's documentation of the feature as announced in late 2025.
- The Dell/Intel Innovation Platform Framework compatibility hold is consistent with a real, previously documented Microsoft safeguard-hold pattern for Dell devices with IPF drivers, and is framed strictly as Microsoft's own notice — no independent claim about Dell hardware is made.
- Post-my-knowledge specifics (the .8875 revision, the July 15 page amendment, current default-on eligibility at 200 GB) rest on the cited KB and Learn pages; all are attributed rather than asserted independently, which is the correct posture.

## Unsupported claims
None found. The piece is notably careful: pause is framed as a short planning tool, not a security strategy ("delaying security fixes has a cost"), and point-in-time restore is explicitly bounded ("does not make updates risk-free," "not a long archive"). Nothing overstates beyond the sources it cites.

## Title, meta, structure, usefulness
- Title, subtitle, and description all accurately reflect the body (pause controls + restore + Dell caution); description is a good length and non-clickbait.
- Structure is clean: framing intro, four H2 sections each ending with its source, consolidated Sources block. The checklist format (check version, check Dell/IPF, check Settings > System > Recovery, pilot-before-rollout for IT) directly serves the stated reader job.
- Cosmetic nit only: the final body section lacks the `---` separator before `## Sources` that the other sections have.

## Image and frontmatter integrity
- `public/images/editorial/2026/07/windows-11-july-update-controls.png` exists; I viewed it — it matches the alt text (laptop with abstract update, calendar, pause, and shield icons, no readable text, so no fake-UI misrepresentation risk), and the attribution honestly discloses it as a generated editorial illustration.
- Slug matches filename, category matches directory, `publishedAt` is today, `status: release-candidate`, author "David Kim" is an established site byline, and "4 min read" fits the ~830-word length.

## Reputational and legal risk
Low. Dell is mentioned only through Microsoft's own compatibility notice (no defamation exposure), the advice never tells readers to skip security updates, and there are no product-disparagement or warranty-adjacent claims.

Two non-blocking follow-ups for the publish step: (1) the pause-updates source URL (`support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/deployment/updates-lifecycle/...`) has a learn.microsoft.com-style path on the support domain — it matches the research artifact, but a live link check before publish would be prudent; (2) the .8875 build revision and July 15 amendment date should be spot-checked against the live KB page since they postdate what I can verify offline. Neither requires a content change to the candidate as written.
